messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 58
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Dentist
  trauma_type: Police violence
  pcl5: 77

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid All Feelings: avoid anything that could cause negative or positive feelings, Avoid Stressors: avoid anything that could be stressful, Checking Surroundings: constantly scan environment for signs of threat
  Threat: Threat from Strangers: I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations, Sleep Problems: Trouble falling or staying asleep, Safe Seat Seeking: I always choose where to sit based on how safe or protected I feel
  Memory: Memory Feels Alien: The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me, Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event., Pain Recall: When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event
  Negative Appraisals: Intrinsic Fault: There is something about me that made the event happen, Life Destroyed: My life has been destroyed by the trauma, Injustice: What happened to me was deeply unfair and nothing has been done about it

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

The night it happened, Marcus was leaving a late dinner with friends in the city. He was fifty-three then, still running his own dental practice, still feeling like he had a handle on things. A patrol car pulled up alongside him as he walked to his car. Two officers jumped out, shouting. Before he could raise his hands or explain he was a dentist, a taxpaying man who had just finished his meal, he was on the ground, his face pressed into the asphalt. He heard the crack of a radio, the grunt of effort, and then the searing pain in his ribs as a knee drove into his side. It was a case of mistaken identity, they said later. A meaningless apology. But Marcus had come to believe that something about him, something intrinsic, had made it happen. *Intrinsic Fault* was a quiet, corrosive certainty that settled into his bones: if he had been a different kind of man, a white man, a man who didn't look like a threat just by existing, the officers would have seen a citizen, not a suspect. What happened was deeply unfair, and nothing had been done about it. *Injustice* wasn't just a thought; it was a pressure in his chest, a grinding resentment that made his jaw ache even before he climbed into his dental chair each morning. He felt that his life had been destroyed by the trauma — *Life Destroyed* — and he often caught himself staring at his own reflection in the operatory mirror, wondering if the man who used to joke with his hygienist was ever coming back.

The memory of that night felt alien, like a film he had been forced to watch rather than something he had lived. *Memory Feels Alien* — he sometimes told his partner that it was like remembering a story about someone else, except this story came with sounds: the *Auditory Recall* of the officer's boots scraping the pavement, the sharp bark of commands. And it came with pain. When the memory returned, often without warning, he felt a phantom ache in his ribs, the same spot where the knee had pinned him down. *Pain Recall* was visceral and humiliating, and it made him feel like he was still on that asphalt. This feeling of the memory being unreal and yet physically present made the negative appraisals worse — *Memory → Negative Appraisals* — because if the memory wasn't even his, how could he ever make sense of it? How could he prove it happened? The injustice felt more profound, his sense of being destroyed more absolute, when the event itself felt like a ghost story he couldn't escape.

Because of these intrusive, painful memories, Marcus began to change how he lived. *Memory → Maladaptive Strategies* — the sounds and the rib pain drove him to avoid anything that could trigger them. He stopped walking anywhere at night. He avoided all feelings, positive or negative. *Avoid All Feelings* was his way of staying safe: if he didn't feel the anger, he couldn't feel the shame. If he didn't feel the love from his partner, he couldn't feel the terror of losing it all. He also avoided anything stressful — *Avoid Stressors* — which meant canceling appointments with anxious patients, delegating difficult procedures to his associate, and gradually shrinking his practice to only the most predictable, low-stakes cases. He started *Checking Surroundings* constantly: every time he entered a room, he mapped the exits, noted the windows, catalogued the faces.

The threat he felt from strangers was pervasive and exhausting. *Threat from Strangers* meant that even a patient walking toward the reception desk made his shoulders tighten. A delivery driver at the back door sent his heart racing. He felt threatened by strangers approaching him even in ordinary situations — a person asking for directions, a neighbor saying hello — and he had developed a habit of *Safe Seat Seeking*: he always chose where to sit based on how safe or protected he felt. In restaurants, his back to a wall. In waiting rooms, a seat with a clear view of the door. At home, he sat on the side of the couch farthest from the windows. This constant vigilance, this scanning for threat, made the memory more accessible — *Threat → Memory* — because every time his heart pounded at an approaching stranger, his brain seemed to say, *Yes, this is what it felt like.* And the memory, in turn, reinforced the threat — *Memory → Threat* — because the pain in his ribs and the sound of boots were proof that danger was real, that it had happened once and could happen again.

The threat also strengthened his negative appraisals. *Threat → Negative Appraisals* — the more he felt threatened by strangers, the more he was certain that something about him had caused the event, that the world saw him as a target. The injustice burned hotter when he was scanning a crowd, because he could see the casual way other people walked, unaware, unafraid. He knew, logically, that not every stranger was a threat, but his body didn't believe it. His body believed that the world was divided into safe and unsafe, and that he was marked.

His maladaptive strategies, in turn, fed back into the memory and the appraisals. *Maladaptive Strategies → Memory* — avoiding all feelings and checking his surroundings meant he was always on alert, and that state of hypervigilance made the memory more likely to surface, as if his brain was saying, *You're scanning for danger, so here's the danger you're looking for.* And *Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals* — the more he avoided, the more he confirmed to himself that his life really was destroyed, that he was too broken to function normally, that the injustice had permanently reshaped him. He had stopped going to his niece's birthday parties. He had stopped having dinner with friends. He told himself it was to avoid stress, but underneath, he was certain that the man who used to laugh at those parties was gone, and that nothing would bring him back.

What finally brought Marcus to seek help was a moment in his own office. A patient, a middle-aged man, walked in wearing a dark uniform. Marcus froze in the hallway, his hand on the door to the operatory. The man was a postal worker, just dropping off a package, but for a few seconds Marcus saw the patrol car, heard the boots. He turned and walked back to his office, closed the door, and sat in the dark for ten minutes. That night, he told his partner he couldn't keep living like this. He was afraid of what he was becoming — a man who was afraid of his own shadow, a dentist who couldn't face a patient in a blue shirt. He was hoping, though he wouldn't say it out loud, that someone could help him find a way to feel like himself again, or at least to stop the pain in his ribs from coming back every time he heard a loud noise.
